record.original_question: What kinds of benchmarking are genuinely useful for evaluating nature-inspired optimization algorithms, and under what conditions, if any, do free lunches exist despite the usual no-free-lunch perspective?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 3. What types of benchmarking are useful? Do free lunches exist, under what conditions?

artifact.category_tag: No Free Lunch theorems and benchmarking
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the setting of black-box optimization, where an algorithm A is a (possibly randomized) procedure that, given access to an objective function f : X → Y from some class F of functions on a finite search space X with values in a finite ordered set Y, sequentially queries points x_1, x_2, … ∈ X, observes values f(x_1), f(x_2), …, and outputs a trace T_m(A,f) = ((x_1,f(x_1)),…,(x_m,f(x_m))) of length m without revisiting points. A performance measure is a function Φ(T_m(A,f)) ∈ ℝ (e.g. best-so-far value), and the average performance of A on a probability distribution P over F is E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))].

The classical No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem states: if P is uniform over the set Y^X of all functions f : X → Y (or, more generally, if P is closed under permutation of X), then for every performance measure Φ depending only on the multiset of observed values, all non-revisiting algorithms A have identical average performance E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))].

Address the following two linked questions for nature-inspired (metaheuristic) optimization algorithms:

(a) Benchmarking. Formulate criteria characterizing which benchmark suites B ⊂ F (finite collections of test functions, possibly with associated distributions and performance measures) yield comparisons of algorithms that are genuinely informative — in the sense of being predictive of performance on unseen problems of practical interest, robust under reasonable transformations (translations, rotations, rescalings, irrelevant variables), and not artificially favoring any particular algorithmic bias. Provide a precise mathematical framework in which such "useful benchmarking" can be defined and verified.

(b) Free lunches. Determine conditions on the function class F, the prior distribution P, the algorithm class 𝒜, and the performance measure Φ under which strict free lunches exist, i.e., there exist algorithms A, A' ∈ 𝒜 with
   E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A,f))] > E_{f∼P}[Φ(T_m(A',f))].
Characterize as completely as possible the structural properties of (F, P) — for instance, non-closure under permutation, restrictions to functions with bounded description length / Kolmogorov complexity, smoothness or Lipschitz constraints, co-evolutionary settings, multi-objective settings, or restrictions on 𝒜 — that admit free lunches, and quantify the maximal achievable gap.
artifact.status_search_result: The original NFL theorems (Wolpert–Macready, 1997) are proved, but follow-up "free lunch" results are still actively investigated: known results include free lunches for co-evolution (Wolpert–Macready 2005), for sets of functions not closed under permutation (Schumacher–Vose–Whitley 2001; Igel–Toussaint 2004), for restricted-complexity function classes (Lattimore–Hutter 2013), and for multi-objective optimization (Corne–Knowles 2003). However, a comprehensive characterization of "useful benchmarking" for nature-inspired algorithms and a complete classification of conditions under which free lunches exist remains an open research direction, frequently cited as an open problem in metaheuristics surveys.

status_evidence.title: No free lunch theorems for optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Wolpert and Macready prove that all algorithms have identical average performance over the set of all functions.

status_evidence.title: Coevolutionary free lunches
status_evidence.snippet: Wolpert and Macready show that, in coevolution, some algorithms outperform others on average.
status_evidence.claim: Free lunches are known to exist in coevolutionary settings.

status_evidence.title: No free lunch and free leftovers theorems for multiobjective optimisation problems
status_evidence.snippet: Corne and Knowles show free lunches exist for multi-objective optimization.
status_evidence.claim: Free lunches exist in multi-objective optimization.

status_evidence.title: No-Free-Lunch theorems and the diversity of algorithms
status_evidence.snippet: Restrictions to function classes of bounded Kolmogorov complexity admit algorithms strictly better than random search.
status_evidence.claim: Free lunches exist when restricting to bounded-complexity functions.
